text: When Rachel saw that she was bearing Jacob no children, she envied her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, "Am I in the place of God, who has kept you from bearing children?"
Then she said, "Here is my servant Bilhah. Sleep with her, so that she may give birth on my knees and I too may be built up through her."
So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Then Rachel said, "God has judged in my favor; he has heard my voice and given me a son." So she named him Dan.
Rachel's servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Then Rachel said, "With a mighty struggle I have wrestled with my sister, and I have won." So she named him Naphtali.

versions.text: Then Rachel said, "I have wrestled mighty wrestlings with my sister, and I have prevailed." So she named him Naphtali.
versions.explanation: "I have wrestled mighty wrestlings" is a stiff, repetitive rendering of the Hebrew cognate construction and reads awkwardly aloud. Recasting the intensifying phrase as an adverbial clause keeps the force of the Hebrew while flowing naturally for oral reading.

text: When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son.
Then Leah said, "Good fortune has come!" So she named him Gad.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Then Leah said, "How happy I am! The women will call me happy." So she named him Asher.
During the wheat harvest Reuben went out and found mandrakes in the field, and he brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."

But she answered her, "Is it a small thing that you took my husband? Will you take my son's mandrakes as well?" "Very well," Rachel said, "he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must come to me, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he slept with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Then Leah said, "God has given me my wages, because I gave my servant to my husband." So she named him Issachar.
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Then Leah said, "God has given me a good gift. This time my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons." So she named him Zebulun.
Later she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son, and she said, "God has taken away my disgrace."
She named him Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add another son to me."
After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me on my way, so I can return to my own place and my own land.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, and let me go. You know how hard I have worked for you."
But Laban said to him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay. I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
And he added, "Name your wages, and I will pay them."
Jacob said to him, "You know how I have served you and how your livestock has fared under my care.
The little you had before I came has increased greatly, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I set my foot. But now, when may I do something for my own household?"
"What shall I give you?" Laban asked. "Don't give me anything," Jacob replied. "But if you will do this one thing for me, I will go on tending and watching over your flocks:
Let me go through all your flocks today and remove from them every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. These will be my wages.

And my honesty will testify for me in the future, whenever you come to check on my wages. Any goat in my possession that is not speckled or spotted, or any lamb that is not dark-colored, will be counted as stolen."
"Agreed," said Laban. "Let it be as you have said."

That same day he removed all the male goats that were streaked or spotted, and all the speckled or spotted female goats—every one that had white on it—and all the dark-colored lambs, and he put them in the care of his sons.
Then he put a three-day journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob continued to tend the rest of Laban's flocks.
Jacob, however, took fresh-cut branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees, and peeled white stripes in them, exposing the white inner wood of the branches.
Then he set the branches he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flocks came to drink, directly in front of the animals. When they came to drink, they bred,
and since they bred in front of the branches, they bore young that were streaked, speckled, or spotted.
Jacob separated the lambs and made the flocks face toward the streaked and dark-colored animals in Laban's flock. He put his own droves by themselves and did not place them with Laban's flock.

versions.text: Jacob set the lambs apart and made the flocks face toward the streaked and dark-colored animals in Laban's flock. So he built up his own herds and kept them separate from Laban's.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says Jacob "placed his own droves by themselves and did not put them with Laban's flock." "Built up his own herds" introduces an idea of increase that is not in the verb שׁית here; the point is separation of ownership, which the corrected wording makes clear.

versions.text: Jacob set the lambs apart and made the flocks face toward the streaked and dark-colored animals in Laban's flock. So he made his own flocks stand alone and did not put them with Laban's animals.
versions.explanation: "Made his own flocks stand alone" is awkward for oral reading and personifies the animals oddly; the verb שׁית here simply means Jacob 'put/placed' his droves by themselves. Rendering both occurrences of שׁית with 'put/place' also preserves the Hebrew repetition, and 'flock' (צֹאן) is more precise than 'animals' at the end. 'Separated' avoids echoing 'apart/alone' twice in the same verse.

text: Whenever the stronger of the flock were breeding, Jacob would set the branches in the troughs before their eyes, so that they would breed near the branches.
But when the animals were feeble, he did not place the branches there. So the weak ones went to Laban and the strong ones to Jacob.

versions.text: But when the animals were weak, he did not put them there. So the weak ones went to Laban and the strong ones to Jacob.
versions.explanation: The pronoun "them" is ambiguous in oral reading: it could be heard as referring to the weak animals rather than the branches. Naming the branches explicitly matches the Hebrew object implied by יָשִׂים (the rods of v. 41) and removes the confusion.

text: In this way the man grew exceedingly prosperous, and he came to own large flocks, as well as female and male servants, camels, and donkeys.
